title: Women Among Top-Cited Scientists: Authorship Patterns, Career Length and Disciplinary Distribution in the 2025 Single-Year Citation Database
content: Background: Women are a minority among highly cited scientists, and it is unclear how those who reach this group differ from men. Methods: We analyzed 159,112 authors in the 2025 single-year database of top-2% scientists whose gender could be inferred from first names (21.1% women). Women and men were compared within Science-Metrix fields using fixed-effects regression, adjusting for career length, publication volume and first-publication cohort. Results: Women were concentrated in Public Health, Social Sciences and Psychology and scarce in Mathematics, Physics and Engineering (dissimilarity index 0.21). Within fields, women had careers 4.4 years shorter, 24% fewer papers, a lower share of single-authored papers (−1.4 percentage points; absent in the first decade of careers and growing thereafter) and less often multi-country careers. Citations per paper were higher, but total citations did not differ after adjustment, and composite scores gave no general evidence that women faced a higher selection bar. Self-citation did not differ; first- and last-author differences disappeared with career stage. Conclusions: Within the top group, differences mostly reflect cohort, volume and field, with a persistent single-authorship gap. Findings are cross-sectional and rely on inferred gender.
